units.translation: Rhipaean mountains, fabulous mountains in Strabo 7 p. 297: those who make myths about the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans. Stephanus of Byzantium: Rhipaia: a mountain of the Hyperboreans, which should rather be written ὄpn, as the scholiast on Sophocles OC 1248 says, from the mountains called Rhipai; but some call them thus, Rhipaean mountains. The ancients disagreed about their location: see Thesaurus vol. 6 p. 2397.
in the scholiast on Sophocles, cited passage: Rhipai indeed of my father.
those who make myths about the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans
Rhipaia: a mountain of the Hyperboreans
from the mountains called Rhipai; but some call them thus, Rhipaean mountains
of a gnat flying with a buzzing sound
I was being roused by the thin beats of a gnat buzzing
such a rush from Zeus comes upon me, causing fear
Thus it has been corrected in the copies from what was first written in M as εἰριμμένος [having been thrown], ει having been made from another letter: which can be ἐρριμμένος [having been thrown].
I threw myself from this rugged rock
and may he hurl my body headlong into dark Tartarus
for having borne me, you cast me into misfortune
who once at me a laughter-provoking missile, the ill-smelling chamber pot, threw
but if you will hurl such harsh and sharpened words
I will not be dishonored by throwing away more (or: by having thrown away more?)
in response to this, let the blazing flame be hurled
upon me let the two-edged lock of fire be hurled
since this boast is not fabricated, but indeed all too true
a man-destroying plague of towers, a shield-throwing ruin
you will crack a bitter-sweet pomegranate
Rhodes, an island of the Carpathian sea
where the Asopus waters the plain with its streams
to the streams of the Euripus
Thus I have corrected for νοθοῦντι [being sluggish], which is in Athenaeus 9 p. 375 c.
with the joint stroke of the dashing oar
and may the wave of the sea with rough surge overwhelm
the gift of earth is borne on worthless surges
the noise of the Persian tongue
whirling the fold of the aegis
the Bosporus, stream of the god
weight, inclination, turn of the scale
weight. Properly said of the weight of a balance sinking downward.
i.e. the onset of divine vengeance, as Schütz interprets it.
such a calamity of suffering came upon them, as to outweigh these things twice in the balance
and the swift turn of Justice's scale watches over those in the light
to gulp down from the living the red libation from their limbs
[The tragedians used long u in all tenses, except that Aeschylus said ῥύεσθε with short u, Sept. 303 824.] to protect, to save
protect the city and the army of Cadmus' race
